related_questions.question: What is the Mohs surgery for basal cell carcinoma?

text_blocks.snippet: Mohs surgery is a highly effective procedure for removing basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer. It's often recommended for BCCs in high-risk areas like the face, or for those that are large, aggressive, or have recurred. The surgery involves removing the tumor layer by layer, with each layer examined under a microscope until all cancerous cells are eliminated. This meticulous approach minimizes the removal of healthy tissue, leading to better cosmetic outcomes and higher cure rates compared to other treatments.
snippet_highlighted_words: Mohs surgery is a highly effective procedure for removing basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer

list.snippet: Local Anesthesia: The area around the tumor is numbed with a local anesthetic.
Initial Removal: The visible tumor and a thin layer of surrounding tissue are removed.
Microscopic Examination: The removed tissue is examined under a microscope to check for cancer cells.
Repeat Removal (if necessary): If cancer cells are found at the edge of the tissue, the surgeon marks the location on a map and removes another layer of tissue only from that specific area.
Repeat until Clear: This process of removing and examining tissue is repeated until all cancerous cells are removed, and the margins are clear.
Wound Closure: Once the tumor is completely removed, the surgeon will discuss options for closing the wound, which may include stitches, flaps, or grafts.

text_blocks.snippet: Why Mohs is Effective for BCC:

list.title: High Cure Rate:
list.snippet: Mohs surgery has a very high cure rate for BCC, especially in high-risk areas.

list.title: Tissue Conservation:
list.snippet: It spares as much healthy tissue as possible, which is crucial for cosmetic and functional outcomes.

list.title: Precision:
list.snippet: The microscopic examination ensures that all cancerous cells are removed, minimizing the chance of recurrence.

list.title: Outpatient Procedure:
list.snippet: Mohs surgery is typically an outpatient procedure, meaning you can go home the same day.

text_blocks.snippet: When is Mohs Surgery Recommended for BCC?

list.snippet: BCCs located on the face, especially around the eyes, nose, lips, or ears.
BCCs that are large, aggressive, or have a high risk of recurrence.
BCCs that have recurred after previous treatments.

text_blocks.snippet: While generally safe, Mohs surgery can have some potential complications, including bruising, bleeding, infection, scarring, or nerve damage. Your surgeon will discuss the risks and benefits of Mohs surgery with you before the procedure.

related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy after Mohs surgery?

text_blocks.snippet: Life expectancy after Mohs surgery is primarily determined by the patient's overall health and the stage of the cancer, rather than the surgery itself. While Mohs surgery is a highly effective treatment for skin cancer, with high cure rates, particularly for basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, it doesn't directly dictate life expectancy. Comorbidities and the patient's age significantly influence survival, with older patients and those with multiple health issues having a shorter life expectancy.
snippet_highlighted_words: primarily determined by the patient's overall health and the stage of the cancer, rather than the surgery itself

list.title: Effectiveness of Mohs Surgery:
list.snippet: Mohs surgery has a very high cure rate for basal and squamous cell carcinomas, with cure rates up to 99% for new cases.

list.title: Impact of Comorbidities:
list.snippet: The age-adjusted Charlson comorbidity index (aCCI) is a strong indicator of survival after Mohs surgery. A study published in Wiley Online Library found that patients with high aCCI scores (≥6) had a significantly shorter median survival compared to those with low scores (aCCI < 6).

list.title: Influence of Age:
list.snippet: In a study of patients aged 90 and older, the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology (JAAD) found that tumor characteristics, defect size, and closure type did not impact survival. However, overall survival was affected by age and comorbidities, according to the study.

list.title: Survival Rates and Melanoma:
list.snippet: For melanoma, survival rates are heavily dependent on the stage of the cancer at diagnosis. For example, the five-year survival rate for Stage I and II melanoma is 98.4%, while it drops to 22.5% for Stage IV.

list.title: Importance of Functional Assessment:
list.snippet: A study by John E. Vine, M.D. emphasizes the importance of considering a patient's functionality when determining the appropriateness of Mohs surgery. A functional assessment can help physicians evaluate a patient's overall health and ability to care for themselves, which is valuable alongside comorbidity assessments.

related_questions.snippet: There are currently two main techniques used for BCC excision, this includes standard excision (SE) and Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) [5]. The difference between the two techniques is how the lesion is excised in a staged manner, with the difference being that there is tissue sparing in MMS.
